av_event.line_text: Tendai: Ha, slowly. That's fair. I do kitchen extensions, first fix, and the amount of times the builder says "planning's fine, planning's fine," and then it's not fine. Then everybody's waiting, and I've got jobs booked back to back, so the whole week goes out the window. That's my fault, really, I book too tight. Natalie tells me.
av_event.what: A teenage boy in a school jumper walks across the kitchen behind Tendai, opens the fridge, takes out a carton of juice, drinks from it standing with the door open, then puts it back and walks out of frame. Tendai doesn't turn round and carries on talking.

text:
B: Alright! Hello, can you hear me okay?
A: Perfectly. You're very clear. I'm Alison.
B: Tendai. Ah, you've got the kitchen as well, I see. Everybody does these from the kitchen table, you know.
A: It's the only room with a decent signal. Also the kettle.
B: Ha, that's the main thing. So where are you, Alison?
A: Tonbridge, in Kent. You?
B: Gloucester. Tuffley. I'm an electrician, self-employed, so I'm in everybody's kitchen all week, and now I'm in my own, it feels like a day off, you know.
A: Do people make you a lot of tea?
B: Oh, don't. There's a lady in Quedgeley, last month, I'm doing her consumer unit, she brings me tea every twenty minutes. Every twenty minutes! By lunchtime I'm, er, I'm shaking, I can't hold the screwdriver. But I can't say no, she's so happy doing it, you know.
A: I'd have been the other sort of customer. Not tea, I'd just want to see what you were doing to my wiring.
B: Ha! Yeah, they stand behind you. What do you do?
A: I'm a planning officer at the council. So I suspect I've been on the receiving end of some of your customers' extensions.
B: Oh, so you're the one saying no!
A: Sometimes. Mostly I'm saying yes, just more slowly than they'd like.
B: Ha, slowly. That's fair. I do kitchen extensions, first fix, and the amount of times the builder says "planning's fine, planning's fine," and then it's not fine. Then everybody's waiting, and I've got jobs booked back to back, so the whole week goes out the window. That's my fault, really, I book too tight. Natalie tells me.
A: Natalie being your wife?
B: Partner. Nine years. We keep saying we'll get married when things calm down. Things don't calm down, you know.
A: Thirty-odd years of marriage hasn't made anything calmer, if that's any comfort. Graham's retired and he's started a project in the hall that's been half-finished since spring.
B: Ah, he's in the club! It's the same with electricians, nothing in our own house gets finished. The lady I spoke to before, her fella's a sparky and she says he's got a switch hanging off the wall.
A: That's reassuring, in a way. It's not just us.
B: Not just you. Do you have kids, Alison?
A: Two, grown up. Bristol and south London. You?
B: Natalie's boy, Kai, he's thirteen. He's my boy, really, you know. I've been there since he was four. He's grown out of his football boots again, that's the third pair this year. I said, Kai, stop growing, I'm not made of money.
A: They don't listen. Mine are both taller than me and I'm still not sure I agreed to it.
B: Ha! And my sister's in Leicester, my mum's still back home in Harare. I try and get back every two, three years.
A: That's a long way to have your mum.
B: It is, yeah. She's getting older, so. Er, you worry. But we talk on WhatsApp nearly every day, she sends me gospel songs, I send her photos of Kai.
A: My mother was forty minutes away and I still didn't visit enough. I'm not sure distance is really the thing.
B: Yeah. Yeah, that's true. Hey, do you go away anywhere nice?
A: Cottages, mostly. Pembrokeshire, Northumberland. Somewhere with a decent pub and nobody else about.
B: That sounds peaceful. We do a caravan in Devon, it's not peaceful at all, Kai's on the —
